text: Nearly every AI governance program organizes around the same four risk categories. This lesson names each one in plain language, no incident report required to make the point.

Bias is a model's outputs systematically favoring or disfavoring some group, in a way that doesn't track what the model is actually supposed to measure. It usually comes from the data reflecting a real-world imbalance, and the model faithfully reproducing it at scale. Privacy risk is the chance an AI system exposes personal information it shouldn't, training data that was never meant to end up in a model, a model prompted into reproducing data it memorized. The model itself can become the exposure, with no traditional breach required.

Security risk covers ways an AI system gets attacked or manipulated, adversarial inputs designed to fool a classification, prompt injection that tricks a generative system into ignoring its instructions, data poisoning during training. Hallucination is specific to generative AI, output that sounds fluent and confident but is factually wrong, because the model is built to produce the most statistically likely next output, not to verify truth, with no mechanism to say I don't know.

These four aren't independent. A biased training set can also be a privacy problem if it overrepresents a vulnerable group. A security attack can be designed specifically to trigger a hallucination. Most of the specific controls in the rest of this course, documentation, access controls, monitoring, incident response, exist because at least one of these four risks is what they're defending against.
Bias, privacy, security, hallucination, four categories, most of this course's controls trace back to one of them. Next up: the roles a real AI governance program assigns to manage all four.
